projects.title: Counsel: Legal Document Proofreading
projects.blurb: Agentic legal proofreading with Google ADK: four parallel Gemini specialists with tools, streaming issues into an ONLYOFFICE DOCX editor.
description: A single LLM pass over a long legal draft mixes spelling, grammar, citations, and formatting in one noisy list. I wanted an agentic setup where narrow specialists run in parallel, call document tools, and stream structured issues a lawyer can review before anything changes in Word.

Counsel orchestrates four Google ADK agents (spelling, grammar, fact/logic, formatting) on Gemini 2.0 Flash. Each agent has its own prompt, tool access (`python-docx` parsing, regex entity extraction, `eyecite` for citations), and SSE stream into a proofreading sidebar. The UI groups issues by agent category; clicking one highlights text in ONLYOFFICE, and “Apply Fix” sends replacements through a custom plugin and iframe bridge. Orgs, cases, and `.docx` uploads live in a FastAPI app with MongoDB GridFS; proofreading runs on a dedicated agent service (port 8001), separate from CRUD and editor callbacks.

Docker Compose ties together React + TypeScript + Tailwind, JWT-signed ONLYOFFICE config, and the two FastAPI services. The agent layer is the product path: parallel runs, tool-grounded findings, and human-in-the-loop edits instead of auto-patching the whole document.

This is an MVP: no real auth (seeded default user), summarizer and sidebar chat are UI placeholders, and quality depends on the agents and tools. I kept a simpler single-prompt `/api/proofread` route on the main backend for comparison; the live panel uses only the ADK agent service.

projects.title: Multi-Label Genre Classifier
projects.blurb: Scraped Smashwords book descriptions and genres, then explored a ~5.8k multi-label dataset ahead of a planned DistilBERT classifier.
description: Books on Smashwords carry several genre tags at once, so a single-label model would miss most of the signal. I wanted a pipeline that collects real descriptions and labels from the site, then trains a transformer that can predict multiple genres from text.

The repo has a scraper and cleaned dataset under `data/` (descriptions paired with genre IDs and a genre map). In `notebooks/data_exploration.ipynb` I mapped IDs to human-readable labels, profiled missing values (~5.5k descriptions across ~5.8k rows), and counted label frequency across hundreds of genres, from broad buckets like Fiction and Nonfiction down to long-tail niches.

The EDA surfaced heavy class imbalance and multi-label overlap (many books share Adventure, Fiction, Romance, etc.), which will drive threshold tuning and evaluation choices before training. Next step is fine-tuning DistilBERT with multi-label sigmoid outputs; modeling code is not started yet.
This is an early-stage project: data collection and exploration are in place, but no trained model or inference API yet.

projects.title: Real-Time 2D Object Recognition
projects.blurb: C++/OpenCV webcam app that segments objects and classifies them with shape features and k-NN or a decision tree.
description: I wanted a lightweight way to recognize everyday objects on a desk in real time, without training a deep network. The challenge is reliable segmentation under changing lighting and clutter, then matching each blob to a class using only geometry.

I built a desktop pipeline in C++17 and OpenCV: blur and adaptive thresholding, morphological cleanup, connected-components labeling, and region tracking with tunable filters (size, boundary ignore, center priority). For each region I compute shape descriptors (area, compactness, aspect ratio, orientation, eccentricity, Hu moments, and an oriented bounding box) and visualize them in separate windows.

A webcam mode lets me add labeled training samples interactively, persist them to a CSV feature database under `dataset/`, and run live classification with bounding boxes, confidence, and an unknown-object threshold. I can switch between nearest-neighbor matching and a custom decision tree built from the same features. A second binary processes still images and saves preprocessed, region, and feature overlays.

I trained and tested on five tabletop classes (book, hat, perfume, scissors, shades). The project sharpened my understanding of classical recognition: feature design, normalization, and tradeoffs between simple classifiers, while keeping the system interactive enough to demo on a live camera feed.

projects.title: Image Processing Application
projects.blurb: Java MVC app with GUI, console, batch script, and async HTTP job server with strategy-based filters/transforms over PPM/BMP/JPG/PNG.
description: For an object-oriented software design course, I needed a system where views, command parsing, and image algorithms stay decoupled, while still supporting interactive editing, scripted batches, and remote job submission.

`Main` routes to four modes: Swing GUI (`GUIView` + `GUIController`), console REPL (`ConsoleView` → `AbstractView` → `ControllerImpl`), batch file (`-file`), and an optional HTTP server. All paths share `AbstractController` command parsing (load, save, flip, split/combine, brighten/darken, dither, etc.). The GUI uses `SwingWorker` for background work, writes rolling `temp_*.png` previews, and injects `GUIController` for histogram export; console and batch use `ControllerImpl` against `ModelImpl` directly.

The model layers `Model` → `ImprovedModel` (filters, transforms, dither) → `EnhancedModel` (histogram). `AbstractModel` keeps a capped `imagesByName` session map (50 images, LRU eviction) and delegates IO to format-specific `BMPImage`, `JPGImage`, `PNGImage`, and `PPMImage` types behind `ImageFactory`. Blur and sharpen use convolution via `ImageFilter` (`BlurFilter`, `SharpenFilter`); greyscale and sepia use matrix transforms via `ImageTransform`, with parallel row/column processing in `AbstractImageTransform`.

I also added an async `ImageProcessingHttpServer` (`GET /health`, `POST /jobs`, `GET /jobs/{id}`) backed by `JobQueueImageProcessingService`, an `ExecutorService` and `LinkedBlockingQueue` where each job spins up its own `ControllerImpl`. Runtime artifacts include `histogram.csv` and a planned `ChartData` hook for GUI charts (not fully wired). JUnit tests mock the model to verify the controller command layer.
